query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a controlled acid-etching and N-doping surface treatment to a near-equiatomic HEA automotive catalyst will form a Pt-rich shell that enhances low-temperature oxidation activity, increases resistance to poisoning (from H2O and NO), and improves long-term durability without increasing overall platinum-group-metal usage.
generation.material_initial_state: Near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element HEA automotive alloy catalyst with uniform elemental distribution and low PGM content.
generation.intervention: Targeted surface modification by controlled acid-etching followed by N-doping.
generation.conditions: Simulated automotive exhaust conditions at low temperatures (below 150 °C), including exposure to typical exhaust poisons (H2O, NO) and undergoing accelerated thermal and chemical aging representative of vehicle lifetime operation.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a Pt-rich surface shell with integrated N atoms that generate strong metal–N bonds, effectively altering the surface electronic structure and enhancing active site stability.
generation.mechanism: Acid-etching preferentially removes less noble elements from the surface, enriching it in Pt. Subsequent N-doping facilitates the formation of metal–N bonds which stabilize the Pt-rich shell, reduce susceptibility to poisoning, and hinder sintering or degradation during thermal cycling.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified HEA catalyst, the modified catalyst is expected to show higher catalytic activity for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation at temperatures below 150 °C, improved resistance to deactivation by H2O and NO, and superior long-term durability under realistic aging conditions.
generation.baseline: The unmodified near-equiatomic HEA catalyst exhibits lower low-temperature activity, increased sensitivity to poisoning species, and noticeable degradation over prolonged exposure to transient exhaust and thermal aging.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only if the treatment conditions are optimized; overly aggressive acid-etching or excessive N-doping may damage the alloy’s core structure or result in undesired changes in composition.
generation.uncertainty: While analogous systems suggest that a Pt-rich shell via acid-etching and N-doping can improve performance, the exact magnitude of improvement under dynamic automotive exhaust conditions remains uncertain until experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two catalyst samples: one set undergoes the controlled acid-etching and N-doping surface treatment, and the other remains as the pristine HEA catalyst. Expose both sets to simulated automotive exhaust conditions at <150 °C with controlled levels of H2O and NO, followed by accelerated thermal and chemical aging cycles. Compare their catalytic performance and surface composition changes.
measurements: Low-temperature oxidation activity (CO and hydrocarbon oxidation rates)
Resistance to poisoning (activity retention in the presence of H2O and NO)
Durability tests (activity retention and structural integrity after aging cycles)
Surface characterization (XPS and HAADF-STEM/EDS) to confirm the formation of a Pt-rich, N-doped shell
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated catalyst does not show statistically significant improvements in low-temperature oxidation activity, poisoning resistance, and durability compared to the unmodified catalyst—or if the anticipated Pt-rich, N-doped shell fails to form—the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: We successfully synthesized the N–Pt/HEA catalyst with a Pt-rich shell and a high entropy alloy PtCoFeNiCu core with multiple M–N bonds via a facile thermal annealing process and an acid-etching de-alloying strategy. The N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst possesses a unique structure and electrochemical stability, resulting in excellent long-term durability under HDV conditions. Detailed studies on atomic structure utilizing in situ synchrotron XRD and XAS, coupled with HAADF-STEM/EDS and DFT calculations, allowed the elucidation of influencing factors on the catalytic properties and performance of the novel catalyst. The high performance of N–Pt/HEA/C originates from the combined effect of high entropy, multiple M-N bonds, and a Pt-rich shell. In addition to the enhancement of corrosion resistance, the M–N bonds through N-doping can boost the activity and durability of the electrocatalyst by the distortion effect in the core structure. The synergy between the three factors further endows the N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst to outperform the state-of-the-art Pt/C electrocatalysts and most binary/ternary Pt-based catalysts for the ORR. reading.lever: Apply a targeted surface modification by controlled acid-etching and N-doping to form a Pt-rich shell on the near-equiatomic HEA catalyst.
reading.why: This intervention, proven in analogous HEA systems for enhanced stability and poisoning-resistance, directly addresses the combined performance requirements while preserving low PGM usage.
